title: Exercise 1
text:
Exercise 1
    Give an example of something we think of as work in everyday circumstances that is not work in the scientific sense. Is energy transferred or changed in form in your example? If so, explain how this is accomplished without doing work.

title: Exercise 2
text:
Exercise 2
    Describe a situation in which a force is exerted for a long time but does no work. Explain.

title: Exercise 3
text:
Exercise 3
    Give an example of a situation in which there is a force and a displacement, but the force does no work. Explain why it does no work.

title: Exercise 4
text:
Exercise 4    
    Work done on a system puts energy into it. Work done by a system removes energy from it. Give an example for each statement.

title: Exercise 5
text:
Exercise 5    
The person in Figure 3.2.1(a) does work on the lawn mower. Under what conditions would the mower gain energy? Under what conditions would it lose energy?

title: Exercise 6
text: Exercise 6A shopper pushes a grocery cart 10 m across a level floor at constant speed, using a horizontal force of 20 N. (a) How much work does the shopper do? (b) What is the net work done on the cart? (c) How much work do the resistive forces do? Explain how your answers are consistent with the cart’s constant speed.

title: Exercise 7
text: Exercise 7A car increases its speed from 30 mph to 60 mph. (a) By what factor does its kinetic energy change? (b) By what factor would its kinetic energy change if its mass doubled while its speed remained unchanged? Explain.

title: Exercise 8
text:
Exercise 8
    When solving for speed in Example 3.3.3, we kept only the positive root. Why?

title: Exercise 9
text: Exercise 9A delivery driver lifts a 10-kg package through a height of 0.50 m to load it into a truck. Use g≈10m/s². (a) By how much does its gravitational potential energy increase? (b) Where does this energy come from? (c) How much work does gravity do on the package? Include the sign.

title: Exercise 10
text:
Exercise 10
    Does the work you do on a book when you lift it onto a shelf depend (a) on the path taken, (b) on the time taken, (c) on the height of the shelf, or (d) on the mass of the book? Briefly explain your answer to each part.

title: Exercise 11
text:
Exercise 11
    In Example 3.4.2, we calculated the final speed of a roller coaster that descended 20 m in height and had an initial speed of 5 m/s downhill. Suppose the roller coaster had had an initial speed of 5 m/s uphill instead, and it coasted uphill, stopped, and then rolled back down to a final point 20 m below the start. Would its final speed be greater than, less than, or equal to the final speed in the original example? Explain in terms of conservation of energy.

title: Exercise 12
text:
Exercise 12
What is a conservative force?

title: Exercise 13
text:
Exercise 13
    What is the relationship of potential energy to conservative force?

title: Exercise 14
text:
Exercise 14
    The force exerted by a diving board is conservative, provided the internal friction is negligible. Assuming friction is negligible, describe changes in the potential energy of a diving board as a swimmer dives from it, starting just before the swimmer steps on the board until just after his feet leave it.

title: Exercise 15
text:
Exercise 15
    Define mechanical energy. What is the relationship of mechanical energy to nonconservative forces? What happens to mechanical energy if only conservative forces act?

title: Exercise 16
text: Exercise 16Consider the two paths in Figure 3.5.1. The toy car is launched with the same spring compression on either path. Assume it reaches the common endpoint on both paths. (a) If friction is negligible, must its final speed be the same on both paths? (b) Must the work done by gravity be the same? (c) If friction is significant, must its final speed still be the same? Briefly explain each answer.

title: Exercise 17
text:
Exercise 17
    List four different forms or types of energy. Give one example of a conversion from each of these forms to another form.

title: Exercise 18
text:
Exercise 18
    List the energy conversions that occur when riding a bicycle.

title: Exercise 19
text:
Exercise 19
    Describe the energy transfers and transformations for a javelin, starting from the point at which an athlete picks up the javelin and ending when the javelin is stuck into the ground after being thrown.

title: Exercise 20
text:
Exercise 20    
    Consider the following scenario. A car for which friction is not negligible accelerates from rest down a hill, running out of gasoline after a short distance. The driver lets the car coast farther down the hill, then up and over a small crest. He then coasts down that hill into a gas station, where he brakes to a stop and fills the tank with gasoline. Identify the forms of energy the car has, and how they are changed and transferred in this series of events. (See Figure 3.E.1.)
        
      
      
    Figure 3.E.1. A car experiencing non-negligible friction coasts down a hill, over a small crest, then downhill again, and comes to a stop at a gas station.

title: Exercise 21
text:
Exercise 21
    Describe a system in which elastic potential energy is stored.

title: Exercise 22
text: Exercise 22A spring is compressed twice as far as before, within the range where Hooke’s law applies. (a) By what factor does the required holding force increase? (b) By what factor does the stored elastic potential energy increase? Explain why the factors differ.

title: Exercise 23
text: Exercise 23Most electrical appliances are rated in watts. Does this rating depend on how long the appliance is on? (When off, it is a zero-watt device.) Explain in terms of the definition of power.

title: Exercise 24
text: Exercise 24A spark of static electricity, such as that you might receive from a doorknob on a cold dry day, may carry a few hundred watts of power. Explain why you are not injured by such a spark.

title: Exercise 25
text: Exercise 25Explain, in terms of the definition of power, why energy consumption is sometimes listed in kilowatt-hours rather than joules. What is the relationship between these two energy units?
